newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Jospin tries to reconcile promises, reality.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Jospin tries to reconcile promises, reality.

text.p: France's Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin began the hard task of reconciling his election promises with economic reality on Thursday, announcing a modest boost to the minimum wage and a gradual move to a 35-hour week.
In a policy speech to parliament that won a standing ovation but dented share prices, Jospin declared: "The commitments made before the French people during the campaign will be honoured."
But he made clear that change would take time because of what he called the "serious" state of public finances.

A planned mini-budget and a national conference on wages, jobs and working hours would be delayed until September to give the government time to study an independent audit of public deficits due in mid-July, he said.
The audit expected to show how far France has strayed from the aim of reducing its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product to qualify for the single European currency from 1999.
Jospin said he was committed to launching the euro on time but, significantly, he made no mention of meeting the tough economic criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
He also stressed that the euro must go hand in hand with economic solidarity to produce growth and jobs and pledged to create the conditions for more vigorous growth at home.

"The feebleness of growth is a problem facing the whole of Europe. There must therefore be a common response. In this perspective, we reaffirm our determination to achieve economic and monetary union at the deadline provided for by the treaty," the prime minister said.

"But you cannot share a currency without creating economic solidarity. The independence of a (European) central bank...does not mean a political vacuum," he said, vowing to press on with France's drive for the European Union to shift policy priorities from austerity to boosting growth and employment.

The Paris stock exchange index fell by 0.7 percent within an hour of his speech but recovered somewhat to end the day 0.44 percent down. Shares in companies involved in privatisations and restructurings fell, while retail shares rose against the trend.
Swept to power in an upset election win three weeks ago, Jospin vowed to give "absolute priority" to a campaign pledge to find 700,000 jobs for young people. But he gave no details.

There were groans of disappointment from the Socialist, Communist and ecologist coalition benches when he announced that the minimum wage, now 6,406 francs a month, would be increased by four percent, far less than trade unions and the Communist party had demanded.
Stung by the reaction, Jospin said that given price rises of less than one percent, this was the biggest boost in purchasing power for the low-paid in 15 years.
He also vowed to end his centre-right predecessors' cuts in jobs in the civil service.

Economist Philippe Brossard of ABN AMRO bank said the smaller-than-expected rise in the minimum wage "shows policy remains slow and cautious..it shows they want to achieve things over a five year period".
But he said it was not clear how Jospin would fund what he called the "long catalogue of expansion measures".

In the austere, schoolmasterly style that is his hallmark, Jospin pledged to restore republican values, introduce morality lessons as well as civics in schools and revive the right of all people born on French soil to automatic citizenship.
"We must return to the republican spirit," he said. "Let's make a pact: a republican pact, a pact for development and for solidarity."

Pledging to review and change immigration and nationality laws enacted by the former centre-right government, he said: "Nothing is more alien to France than xenophobia and racism. France must define a firm, dignified immigration policy without renouncing its values or compromising its social balance."

Jospin promised to free the justice system from political meddling, leaving the appointment of investigating judges and prosecutors in the hands of an independent council and barring the Justice Ministry from intervening in individual cases.
The Socialist leader said his government aimed to stabilise the overall tax burden. "If growth allows it, my target is to reduce it in the longer term," he said.

Jospin said his government did not favour privatisations of telecommunications, electronics or aerospace companies, but accepted that they needed to adapt and form partnerships with other European companies.

"In the absence of a justification based on the national interest, we are not favourable to the privatisation of this shared heritage that the big state enterprises in competitive industries represent," he said.
